questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message ending with:
   Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.

   Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message ending with:
   Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.

   Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- You must use your `Read` tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file.
- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: line number + tab. Everything after that is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file. Either provide a larger string with more surrounding context to make it unique or use `replace_all` to change every instance of `old_string`.
- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

1	package viewer
2	
3	import (
4		"log"
5		"time"
6	
7		"github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles/spinner"
8		tea "github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea"
9	
10		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/ui/keymap"
11		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/viewer"
12	)
13	
14	// Init loads the source, if there is one.
15	func (m Model) Init() tea.Cmd {
16		if m.source == nil {
17			return nil
18		}
19		return tea.Batch(loadCmd(m.source), m.spinner.Tick)
20	}
21	
22	// loadCmd fetches a source's content. Every read the viewer does goes through
23	// here, on a command's goroutine — Update does no I/O (Rule 110).
24	func loadCmd(source viewer.Source) tea.Cmd {
25		return func() tea.Msg {
26			data, err := source.Load()
27			return DocumentLoadedMsg{
28				Name:    source.Name(),
29				Kind:    source.Kind(),
30				Content: data,
31				Err:     err,
32			}
33		}
34	}
35	
36	// followTickMsg asks for the next read of a followed source. It carries the
37	// generation it was started for, so a loop the user has stopped cannot
38	// resurrect itself — see stopFollowing.
39	type followTickMsg struct{ gen int }
40	
41	func followTickCmd(every time.Duration, gen int) tea.Cmd {
42		// A non-positive interval would make tea.Tick fire without pausing and spin
43		// one docker exec per frame. Refused here rather than trusted, the way the
44		// ports tab refuses a hand-edited 0.
45		if every <= 0 {
46			every = defaultFollowInterval
47		}
48		return tea.Tick(every, func(time.Time) tea.Msg { return followTickMsg{gen: gen} })
49	}
50	
51	// defaultFollowInterval is the floor a source with no sensible answer falls to.
52	const defaultFollowInterval = 2 * time.Second
53	
54	// InEditMode keeps command mode out while a field has the keyboard: the search
55	// box, or the go-to-line prompt.
56	func (m Model) InEditMode() bool { return m.bar.InEditMode() || m.gotoActive }
57	
58	// FilterBarVisible tells the router to close the viewport border into the bar
59	// (Rule 136).
60	func (m Model) FilterBarVisible() bool {
61		// Every display but the tree is text, and the search belongs to all of
62		// them: a rendered Markdown is searched on what it shows, which is the only
63		// answer that agrees with the screen.
64		//
65		// The go-to-line prompt takes the same slot, so it closes the border the
66		// same way — and the footer stands at the same height whether the prompt
67		// opened over an active search or over nothing.
68		return (m.bar.IsVisible() || m.gotoActive) && m.display != displayTree
69	}
70	
71	func (m Model) Update(msg tea.Msg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
72		switch msg := msg.(type) {
73		case tea.WindowSizeMsg:
74			m.resize(msg.Width, msg.Height)
75			return m, nil
76	
77		case tea.KeyMsg:
78			return m.handleKeyMsg(msg)
79	
80		case DocumentLoadedMsg:
81			return m.handleDocumentLoaded(msg)
82	
83		case PagerExitMsg:
84			return m.handlePagerExit(msg)
85	
86		case followTickMsg:
87			return m.handleFollowTick(msg)
88	
89		case spinner.TickMsg:
90			// The chain stops when nothing is loading, and Init/reload restart it.
91			if !m.loading {
92				return m, nil
93			}
94			var cmd tea.Cmd
95			m.spinner, cmd = m.spinner.Update(msg)
96			m.footer.SetSpinnerFrame(m.spinner.View())
97			return m, cmd
98		}
99	
100		m.footer.Handle(msg)
101		return m, nil
102	}
103	
104	// resize lays out whichever half is on screen. Both are sized, not just the
105	// active one: a `f` between two window sizes would otherwise show a pane laid
106	// out for the previous width.
107	func (m *Model) resize(width, height int) {
108		m.width = width
109		m.height = height
110	
111		m.tree.Resize(width, height)
112	
113		m.textViewport.Width = width
114		m.textViewport.Height = max(height, 1)
115		m.bar.Resize(width)
116		m.rebuildText() // the wrap and the padding both depend on the width
117	}
118	
119	func (m Model) handleDocumentLoaded(msg DocumentLoadedMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
120		m.loading = false
121		if msg.Err != nil {
122			log.Printf("ERROR [viewer] load %s: %v", msg.Name, msg.Err)
123			return m, m.footer.Error(loadErrorMessage(msg.Err))
124		}
125		m.footer.Clear()
126		return m, m.applyDocument(viewer.Open(msg.Name, msg.Kind, msg.Content))
127	}
128	
129	// loadErrorMessage names the two refusals and hides the rest behind the log
130	// (Rule 128): "file is too large" is something the user can act on, an OS error
131	// string in a footer is not.
132	func loadErrorMessage(err error) string {
133		switch err {
134		case viewer.ErrTooLarge:
135			return "File is too large to view"
136		case viewer.ErrBinary:
137			return "Not a text file"
138		default:
139			return "Failed to open — check logs"
140		}
141	}
142	
143	// handlePagerExit takes the pager's return, and says so when it failed.
144	//
145	// The report is not decoration. A pager that cannot start comes back in
146	// milliseconds and looks exactly like one the user quit at once, so the whole
147	// event is indistinguishable from `V` doing nothing — which is precisely how the
148	// broken Windows command line went unnoticed. The log line was already there and
149	// nobody reads a log to find out why a key did nothing.
150	func (m Model) handlePagerExit(msg PagerExitMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
151		var report tea.Cmd
152		if msg.Err != nil {
153			log.Printf("ERROR [viewer] pager: %v", msg.Err)
154			report = m.footer.Error("Pager failed — check logs")
155		}
156		// Whatever the pager showed, the document may have moved on while the TUI
157		// was suspended. Reloading is the only way back to something true.
158		if m.source == nil {
159			return m, report
160		}
161		m.loading = true
162		return m, tea.Batch(report, loadCmd(m.source))
163	}
164	
165	func (m Model) handleKeyMsg(msg tea.KeyMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
166		// The prompt is a mode: it claims every key before the pane sees one, the
167		// way a confirmation modal does, so a digit cannot also scroll and `esc`
168		// closes the prompt rather than leaving the viewer.
169		if m.gotoActive {
170			return m.handleGotoKey(msg)
171		}
172		if m.bar.InEditMode() {
173			var cmd tea.Cmd
174			m.bar, cmd = m.bar.Update(msg)
175			m.rebuildText()
176			return m, cmd
177		}
178	
179		switch msg.String() {
180		case "esc":
181			return m.goBack()
182		case "f":
183			m.toggleDisplay()
184			return m, nil
185		case "c":
186			m.toggleHighlight()
187			return m, nil
188		case "ctrl+r":
189			return m.reload()
190		}
191	
192		if m.display == displayTree {
193			return m.handleTreeKey(msg)
194		}
195		return m.handleTextKey(msg)
196	}
197	
198	// goBack returns to whoever opened the document. With no origin — the empty
199	// viewer the router builds for its own contract test — there is nowhere to go,
200	// and swallowing esc silently is better than switching to a view nobody asked
201	// for.
202	func (m Model) goBack() (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
203		if m.OriginView == "" {
204			return m, nil
205		}
206		// Leaving stops the clock. The router keeps this view, so a loop left
207		// running would go on shelling out to docker every two seconds for a
208		// document nobody is looking at — and the user would come back to a pane
209		// that had scrolled itself to the bottom while they were gone.
210		m = m.stopFollowing()
211		origin := m.OriginView
212		return m, func() tea.Msg { return BackToOriginMsg{Origin: origin} }
213	}
214	
215	func (m Model) reload() (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
216		if m.source == nil {
217			return m, nil
218		}
219		m.loading = true
220		return m, tea.Batch(loadCmd(m.source), m.spinner.Tick)
221	}
222	
223	func (m Model) handleTreeKey(msg tea.KeyMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
224		switch msg.String() {
225		case "right":
226			m.toggleNode(true)
227			return m, nil
228		case "left":
229			m.toggleNode(false)
230			return m, nil
231		}
232		return m, m.tree.Update(msg)
233	}
234	
235	func (m Model) handleTextKey(msg tea.KeyMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
236		switch msg.String() {
237		case "/":
238			return m, m.bar.ActivateSearch()
239		case "s":
240			m.toggleCaseSensitive()
241			return m, nil
242		case "n":
243			m.toggleLineNumbers()
244			return m, nil
245		case "g":
246			return m, m.activateGoto()
247		case "w":
248			m.wrap = !m.wrap
249			m.rebuildText()
250			return m, nil
251		case "v":
252			if !m.isLog() {
253				return m, nil
254			}
255			m.cycleVerbosity()
256			return m, nil
257		case "t":
258			return m.toggleTimestamps()
259		case keymap.Fetch:
260			return m.toggleFollow()
261		case keymap.Pager:
262			return m.openPager()
263	
264		// The scroll keys. `q` is deliberately absent: it is the application's quit
265		// key (Rule 111), and the logs pane this replaced was the one screen that
266		// swallowed it.
267		case "up":
268			m.textViewport.ScrollUp(1)
269		case "down":
270			m.textViewport.ScrollDown(1)
271		case "pgup":
272			m.textViewport.HalfPageUp()
273		case "pgdown":
274			m.textViewport.HalfPageDown()
275		case "home":
276			m.textViewport.GotoTop()
277		case "end":
278			m.textViewport.GotoBottom()
279		}
280		return m, nil
281	}
282	
283	// ── The source's optional capabilities ───────────────────────────────────────
284	//
285	// Each is probed with a type assertion, the way the router probes FooterView.
286	// They are three single-method interfaces rather than one with three methods
287	// precisely so there is no half-satisfied state: CLAUDE.md's HeaderView warning
288	// is about a view supplying two of four methods and silently satisfying none.
289	
290	// timestamps returns the source's timestamp capability, if it has one.
291	func (m Model) timestamps() (viewer.Timestamped, bool) {
292		src, ok := m.source.(viewer.Timestamped)
293		return src, ok
294	}
295	
296	func (m Model) followable() (viewer.Followable, bool) {
297		src, ok := m.source.(viewer.Followable)
298		return src, ok
299	}
300	
301	func (m Model) pageable() (viewer.Pageable, bool) {
302		src, ok := m.source.(viewer.Pageable)
303		return src, ok
304	}
305	
306	// timestampsOn tracks the toggle rather than asking the source, which holds it
307	// but cannot be interrogated through the interface — WithTimestamps returns a
308	// new source rather than mutating one, so nothing is shared with a command
309	// already in flight (Rule 110).
310	func (m Model) toggleTimestamps() (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
311		src, ok := m.timestamps()
312		if !ok {
313			return m, nil
314		}
315		m.showTimestamps = !m.showTimestamps
316		m.source = src.WithTimestamps(m.showTimestamps)
317		m.loading = true
318		return m, loadCmd(m.source)
319	}
320	
321	// toggleFollow is `F`. It re-reads the source on its own clock, into this pane.
322	//
323	// It used to be tea.ExecProcess over `docker logs -f`, and the defect that
324	// replaced it is worth keeping written down: the only way out of that process
325	// is ctrl+c, a suspended TUI does not intercept it, so it killed DevDesk and
326	// gave the terminal back in whatever mode the child had left it — after which
327	// keys stopped answering. A capability whose only exit kills the application is
328	// not one.
329	//
330	// The read is the one `ctrl+r` already does: same command, same message, same
331	// handler. Following is that key on a timer and nothing more, which is why it
332	// costs no new loading path.
333	func (m Model) toggleFollow() (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
334		src, ok := m.followable()
335		if !ok {
336			return m, nil
337		}
338		if m.following {
339			return m.stopFollowing(), nil
340		}
341		m.following = true
342		m.followGen++
343		// The first read is immediate. Waiting a whole interval before anything
344		// moves would leave the user unsure the key did anything, and what is on
345		// screen is already up to one interval old.
346		return m, tea.Batch(loadCmd(m.source), followTickCmd(src.FollowInterval(), m.followGen))
347	}
348	
349	// stopFollowing is the one place following is turned off, so no path can leave
350	// the flag set with no tick behind it, or a tick running with the flag clear.
351	func (m Model) stopFollowing() Model {
352		m.following = false
353		// Bumping the generation is what actually ends the loop. The tick already
354		// in flight blocks for its whole interval and arrives whatever happens
355		// here; the mismatch is what makes it a no-op instead of it finding the
356		// flag turned back on and carrying a second loop into the new run.
357		m.followGen++
358		return m
359	}
360	
361	// handleFollowTick re-reads, then schedules the next one.
362	//
363	// A stale tick — from a loop the user stopped, or restarted — returns no
364	// command, which is how the old loop dies rather than running beside the new.
365	func (m Model) handleFollowTick(msg followTickMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
366		if !m.following || msg.gen != m.followGen || m.source == nil {
367			return m, nil
368		}
369		src, ok := m.followable()
370		if !ok {
371			return m.stopFollowing(), nil
372		}
373		// m.loading stays false deliberately: a load is reported in the footer with
374		// a spinner (Rule 139), and one blinking every two seconds would read as
375		// something going wrong with the thing that is working. The follow status
376		// line is what says the pane is live.
377		return m, tea.Batch(loadCmd(m.source), followTickCmd(src.FollowInterval(), msg.gen))
378	}
379	
380	// openPager hands the document to the system pager.
381	//
382	// It survives for one source and deliberately: `less` handles a gigabyte and
383	// follows it, which a viewport holding the whole document in memory never will.
384	// Every other pager path in the application is gone.
385	func (m Model) openPager() (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
386		src, ok := m.pageable()
387		if !ok {
388			return m, nil
389		}
390		return m, tea.ExecProcess(src.PagerCmd(), func(err error) tea.Msg {
391			return PagerExitMsg{Err: err}
392		})
393	}

3	import (
4		"github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles/spinner"
5		"github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles/textinput"
6		"github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles/viewport"
7		tea "github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea"

15	)

17	// display is how the document is shown.
18	//
19	// One axis, and `f` is the only thing that moves along it: the document as it
20	// is, against the one derived view its kind has. A kind has at most one — a tree
21	// when it is Structured, a rendered form when it is Renderable — so the toggle
22	// stays binary at every moment even though there are three values here.
23	//
24	// "Plain text" is still not one of them. It is this pane with the colour off,
25	// and giving it a display of its own would make one screen reachable two ways —
26	// the shape §3.9 removed from the secret backend and the deleted `:theme`
27	// command took with it.
28	type display int
29	
30	const (
31		displayTree display = iota
32		displayText
33		displayRendered
34	)
35	
36	// Model is the document viewer.
37	type Model struct {
38		config *config.Config
39		width  int
40		height int
41	
42		// source is where the document came from, and it is kept rather than
43		// discarded after the first read: reload, follow and the timestamps toggle
44		// are all questions for the origin, not for the bytes.
45		source  viewer.Source
46		doc     viewer.Document
47		loading bool
48		// spinner turns while the document is being read. The load is reported in
49		// the footer, so the pane keeps whatever it was already showing.
50		spinner spinner.Model
51	
52		display   display
53		highlight bool
54		wrap      bool
55		minLevel  viewer.Level
56		// showLineNumbers draws the gutter. Off by default: it spends width on
57		// every line of the pane to answer a question most readings never ask.
58		showLineNumbers bool
59		// caseSensitive is the mode the `/` filter runs in. Nothing reads it but
60		// the one call to viewer.MatchRanges, which answers both which lines
61		// survive and which spans are highlighted — a second reading of this flag
62		// could only be a way for those two to disagree.
63		caseSensitive bool
64		// showTimestamps is tracked here rather than asked of the source:
65		// WithTimestamps returns a new source instead of mutating one, so nothing is
66		// shared with a command already in flight (Rule 110), and there is therefore
67		// nothing to read the flag back off.
68		showTimestamps bool
69	
70		// following re-reads the source on its own clock, into this pane. It
71		// replaced a `docker logs -f` run through tea.ExecProcess, which could only
72		// be left with ctrl+c — killing the application and handing the terminal
73		// back in the child's mode.
74		following bool
75		// followGen invalidates a tick loop the user has already stopped.
76		//
77		// tea.Tick blocks for its whole interval, so a tick scheduled before `F`
78		// turned following off still arrives after it; turning follow back on before
79		// that one lands would leave two loops running and double the read rate for
80		// the life of the view. A stale tick is the one that fails to match this.
81		followGen int
82	
83		// The tree half.
84		tree      datatable.Model[treeRow]
85		collapsed map[int]bool
86	
87		// The text half. lines is the document cut into token spans; it is rebuilt
88		// when the document loads and when `c` toggles, never per frame.
89		lines        []docLine
90		textViewport viewport.Model
91		bar          components.FilterBar
92		matchedLines int
93	
94		// rowOfLine is where each document line landed in the rendered pane, by
95		// line number. It is the only thing that knows: a row is not a line once a
96		// filter has dropped some and a wrap has split others, and `g` needs the
97		// answer after both. Rebuilt with the pane, so it never describes an older
98		// one.
99		rowOfLine map[int]int
100	
101		// The go-to-line prompt. It takes the filter bar's slot for as long as it
102		// is open — see RenderFooter — so the footer's height does not change when
103		// it opens over an active search.
104		gotoInput  textinput.Model
105		gotoActive bool
106	
107		// OriginView is where esc returns to. The router sets it from whatever view
108		// asked for the document.
109		OriginView command.ViewType
110	
111		footer components.FooterMessage
112	}
113	
114	// New builds an empty viewer.
115	//
116	// It exists so the router can create the view like any other — the contract test
117	// builds every view and asks it for a title and its shortcuts. On screen it says
118	// there is nothing open, which is the truth and is only ever reached by opening
119	// the view without a document.
120	func New(cfg *config.Config) Model {
121		s := spinner.New()
122		s.Spinner = spinner.Dot
123		s.Style = theme.SpinnerStyle()
124	
125		gi := textinput.New()
126		theme.StyleTextInput(&gi)
127		// A line number and nothing else: the field refuses anything but digits, so
128		// the parse below it cannot be handed something it has to explain.
129		gi.CharLimit = gotoDigitLimit
130		gi.Validate = digitsOnly
131	
132		return Model{
133			spinner:      s,
134			config:       cfg,
135			highlight:    true,
136			collapsed:    make(map[int]bool),
137			tree:         datatable.New(datatable.Config[treeRow]{Columns: treeColumns(), SortColumn: -1}),
138			textViewport: viewport.New(0, 0),
139			bar:          components.NewFilterBar(),
140			gotoInput:    gi,
141			rowOfLine:    make(map[int]int),
142			display:      displayText,
143		}
144	}
145	
146	// NewWithSource builds a viewer that will load this source when it starts.
147	func NewWithSource(cfg *config.Config, source viewer.Source) Model {
148		m := New(cfg)
149		m.source = source
150		m.loading = true
151		return m
152	}
153	
154	// Name is what the header calls the document.
155	func (m Model) Name() string {
156		if m.doc.Name != "" {
157			return m.doc.Name
158		}
159		if m.source != nil {
160			return m.source.Name()
161		}
162		return ""
163	}
164	
165	// hasDocument reports whether anything has been loaded. Most of the keys and
166	// every shortcut but esc are conditional on it (Rule 130).
167	func (m Model) hasDocument() bool {
168		return m.doc.Name != "" || m.doc.Text != ""
169	}
170	
171	// structured reports whether the tree display is available at all.
172	func (m Model) structured() bool {
173		return m.doc.Kind.Structured() && m.doc.Root != nil
174	}
175	
176	// renderable reports whether the rendered display is available at all.
177	func (m Model) renderable() bool {
178		return m.doc.Kind.Renderable()
179	}
180	
181	// derived is the display this document has besides its own text, and whether it
182	// has one at all.
183	//
184	// One function so that `f`, the opening display and the shortcuts all read the
185	// same answer. Three call sites deciding it with their own switch is how a view
186	// ends up offering a display it will then refuse to show (Rule 130).
187	func (m Model) derived() (display, bool) {
188		switch {
189		case m.structured():
190			return displayTree, true
191		case m.renderable():
192			return displayRendered, true
193		default:
194			return displayText, false
195		}
196	}
197	
198	// isLog reports whether the verbosity filter applies.
199	func (m Model) isLog() bool { return m.doc.Kind == viewer.KindLog }
200	
201	// applyDocument installs a freshly parsed document and settles every piece of
202	// state that depends on it.
203	//
204	// One function rather than a handful of assignments at the call sites: a
205	// document arrives from a first load, from a reload and from a timestamps
206	// toggle, and a display left pointing at a tree that the new document does not
207	// have would render an empty pane with nothing to say why.
208	//
209	// It returns the footer message's expiry timer, which the caller must pass on:
210	// a message set without one never clears (Rule 128).
211	func (m *Model) applyDocument(doc viewer.Document) tea.Cmd {
212		m.doc = doc
213		m.loading = false
214		m.collapsed = make(map[int]bool)
215	
216		// A document opens on its derived display when it has one, which is what
217		// the request asked for: a .json opens as json, a .xml as xml, a .md as the
218		// document it is meant to read as. `f` is there for the source.
219		m.display, _ = m.derived()
220	
221		// The spans come after the display, not before: a rendered document is a
222		// different token stream from its source, so which one to build is the
223		// display's answer to give.
224		m.lines = buildLines(doc, m.highlight, m.display == displayRendered)
225	
226		// A verbosity filter left over from a previous document would hide lines of
227		// this one for a reason the user set on something else.
228		if !m.isLog() {
229			m.minLevel = viewer.LevelUnknown
230		}
231		m.syncFilterTokens()
232	
233		m.rebuildTree()
234		m.tree.GotoTop()
235		m.rebuildText()
236	
237		// A followed document lands at the bottom, where the new lines are. Every
238		// other arrival lands at the top: a first load, a reload and a timestamps
239		// toggle are all "here is the document", and the document starts at line
240		// one. Following is the one case where the interesting end is the other one,
241		// and a re-read that jumped back to the top every two seconds would make the
242		// pane unusable for exactly what it was turned on for.
243		if m.following {
244			m.textViewport.GotoBottom()
245		} else {
246			m.textViewport.GotoTop()
247		}
248	
249		// A warning, not an error: nothing failed, the document simply cannot be
250		// shown the way its name asked for.
251		if doc.ParseErr != nil {
252			return m.footer.Warn("Malformed " + doc.Name + " — showing text")
253		}
254		return nil
255	}
256	
257	// toggleHighlight is `c`. It rebuilds the spans, which is the one thing that
258	// costs anything here — and the reason it is a key rather than something
259	// recomputed on every frame.
260	func (m *Model) toggleHighlight() {
261		m.highlight = !m.highlight
262		m.lines = buildLines(m.doc, m.highlight, m.display == displayRendered)
263		m.rebuildTree()
264		m.rebuildText()
265	}
266	
267	// toggleLineNumbers is `n`. The spans are untouched — the gutter is not a token
268	// and never enters the text a search is run against — so only the pane is
269	// rendered again.
270	func (m *Model) toggleLineNumbers() {
271		m.showLineNumbers = !m.showLineNumbers
272		m.rebuildText()
273	}
274	
275	// toggleCaseSensitive is `s`. It re-filters the query already in force rather
276	// than asking for it again: the mode is a property of the search, not of the
277	// typing, and a toggle that cleared the query would make comparing the two
278	// readings — the whole reason to press it — a matter of retyping.
279	func (m *Model) toggleCaseSensitive() {
280		m.caseSensitive = !m.caseSensitive
281		m.syncFilterTokens()
282		m.rebuildText()
283	}
284	
285	// toggleDisplay is `f`. It does nothing for a document with no derived display,
286	// and the shortcut is hidden in that case rather than offered and ignored.
287	//
288	// It rebuilds the spans when it crosses the rendered boundary, because the two
289	// sides are not the same tokens: the rendered form is the stream with its
290	// markers taken out. The tree costs nothing here — it reads the parsed nodes,
291	// not these lines.
292	func (m *Model) toggleDisplay() {
293		derived, ok := m.derived()
294		if !ok {
295			return
296		}
297		if m.display == derived {
298			m.display = displayText
299		} else {
300			m.display = derived
301		}
302	
303		if derived == displayRendered {
304			m.lines = buildLines(m.doc, m.highlight, m.display == displayRendered)
305			m.rebuildText()
306			m.textViewport.GotoTop()
307		}
308	}
309	
310	// formatLabel is what the header prints: the kind and the display, and the
311	// filter when there is one.
312	func (m Model) formatLabel() string {
313		if !m.hasDocument() {
314			return "-"
315		}
316		label := m.doc.Kind.String()
317		if m.structured() {
318			if m.display == displayTree {
319				return label + " · tree"
320			}
321			return label + " · text"
322		}
323		if m.renderable() {
324			if m.display == displayRendered {
325				return label + " · rendered"
326			}
327			return label + " · raw"
328		}
329		if m.isLog() && m.minLevel != viewer.LevelUnknown {
330			return label + " · " + minLevelLabel(m.minLevel)
331		}
332		return label
333	}

1	package viewer
2	
3	import (
4		"fmt"
5		"strings"
6	
7		"github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss"
8	
9		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/ui/components"
10		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/ui/help"
11		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/ui/keymap"
12		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/ui/shortcut"
13		"github.com/anthnel/devdesk/internal/ui/theme"
14	)
15	
16	// View renders whichever half is on screen.
17	func (m Model) View() string {
18		contentStyle := lipgloss.NewStyle().Background(theme.ColorBackground).PaddingLeft(1)
19	
20		switch {
21		case m.loading && !m.hasDocument():
22			// The load says so in the footer, with a spinner. Nothing is shown here
23			// because there is nothing yet to show — and a reload keeps the
24			// document on screen rather than blanking it, which is the case below.
25			return ""
26		case !m.hasDocument():
27			return contentStyle.Render(theme.HelpStyle.Render("\nNothing open\n\nOpen a file from workspaces, or inspect a container."))
28		case m.display == displayTree:
29			return m.tree.View()
30		default:
31			return m.textViewport.View()
32		}
33	}
34	
35	// GetFooterHeight is Rule 124's budget: an empty line and an info line, plus the
36	// filter bar when it is showing.
37	//
38	// The go-to-line prompt shares that slot with the filter bar and the two never
39	// hold it at once, so the height is the same whichever is there — which is what
40	// keeps the pane from resizing under the reader when the prompt opens over an
41	// active search.
42	func (m Model) GetFooterHeight() int {
43		return 2 + m.barHeight()
44	}
45	
46	func (m Model) barHeight() int {
47		if m.gotoActive {
48			return 2
49		}
50		return m.bar.ExtraHeight()
51	}
52	
53	// RenderFooter draws the bar and the one line of state.
54	func (m Model) RenderFooter(width int) string {
55		var parts []string
56		switch {
57		case m.gotoActive:
58			parts = append(parts, m.renderGotoBar(width))
59		case m.bar.IsVisible():
60			parts = append(parts, m.bar.View())
61		}
62		parts = append(parts, theme.EmptyLineBg(width), m.footer.View(width, m.status()))
63		return strings.Join(parts, "\n")
64	}
65	
66	// status is what the view derives on every frame: the read, reported here so
67	// the pane does not swap itself for a message.
68	func (m Model) status() components.Status {
69		if m.loading {
70			return components.Status{Text: "Loading " + m.Name() + "...", Spinner: true}
71		}
72		// Following is a state, not an event, so it is derived here rather than
73		// posted as a footer message — one would expire after three seconds while
74		// the pane went on refreshing (Rule 128). It is also the only thing on
75		// screen saying the document is live: the reads themselves are deliberately
76		// silent, because a spinner blinking every two seconds would read as
77		// something going wrong with the thing that is working.
78		if m.following {
79			return components.Status{Text: "Following — " + keymap.Fetch + " to stop"}
80		}
81		return components.Status{}
82	}
83	
84	// ── HeaderView ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
85	//
86	// All four methods. The router probes for the interface as a whole and falls
87	// back in silence, so a view supplying two of them renders an empty title with
88	// nothing to say why — which is what happened to the configuration view.
89	
90	func (m Model) GetTitle() string {
91		if name := m.Name(); name != "" {
92			return theme.IconCodeFile + " Viewer · " + name
93		}
94		return theme.IconCodeFile + " Viewer"
95	}
96	
97	func (m Model) GetIcon() string { return "" }
98	
99	func (m Model) GetHeaderInfo(context string) []shortcut.HeaderInfo {
100		info := []shortcut.HeaderInfo{
101			{Key: "Context", Value: context, Style: theme.HeaderValueStyle},
102			{Key: "Format", Value: m.formatLabel(), Style: theme.HeaderValueStyle},
103		}
104		if !m.hasDocument() {
105			return info
106		}
107		if m.structured() && m.display == displayTree {
108			return append(info, shortcut.HeaderInfo{
109				Key: "Nodes", Value: fmt.Sprintf("%d", m.doc.NodeCount()), Style: theme.HeaderValueStyle,
110			})
111		}
112		return append(info, shortcut.HeaderInfo{
113			Key: "Lines", Value: m.lineCount(), Style: theme.HeaderValueStyle,
114		})
115	}
116	
117	// lineCount says how many lines are showing, and out of how many when a filter
118	// is narrowing them. A bare count under an active filter would read as the size
119	// of the document, which is the one thing it is not.
120	func (m Model) lineCount() string {
121		total := len(m.lines)
122		if m.matchedLines == total {
123			return fmt.Sprintf("%d", total)
124		}
125		return fmt.Sprintf("%d/%d", m.matchedLines, total)
126	}
127	
128	// GetShortcuts is state-aware (Rule 130): every key that depends on the kind of
129	// document or on what its source can do is offered only when it would work.
130	func (m Model) GetShortcuts() shortcut.Shortcuts {
131		if !m.hasDocument() {
132			return []shortcut.Shortcut{{Key: "esc", Description: "Go back"}}
133		}
134	
135		var shortcuts []shortcut.Shortcut
136	
137		if m.structured() {
138			// ←→ collapses a node, which only the tree has — greyed in the text
139			// pane rather than dropped, for the same reason as w and / below.
140			inTree := m.display == displayTree
141			display := "Show as tree"
142			if inTree {
143				display = "Show as text"
144			}
145			shortcuts = append(shortcuts,
146				shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "←→", Description: "Collapse/Expand", Disabled: !inTree},
147				shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "f", Description: display},
148			)
149		}
150	
151		// The same key, and the wording says which way it goes — "Show raw" on a
152		// rendered document, "Show rendered" on its source.
153		if m.renderable() {
154			if m.display == displayRendered {
155				shortcuts = append(shortcuts, shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "f", Description: "Show raw markdown"})
156			} else {
157				shortcuts = append(shortcuts, shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "f", Description: "Show rendered markdown"})
158			}
159		}
160	
161		// The tree is the same document seen another way, and `f` toggles between
162		// the two — so the text pane's keys are greyed there rather than dropped
163		// (Rule 130). Hiding them made three entries appear and disappear on every
164		// press of a key whose whole job is to switch back and forth.
165		//
166		// What depends on the *document* rather than on the display stays out of
167		// the list entirely: a Markdown file has no verbosity and never will, which
168		// is a different screen's worth of difference, not a "not now".
169		inTree := m.display == displayTree
170		shortcuts = append(shortcuts, shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "w", Description: "Toggle wrap", Disabled: inTree})
171		if m.isLog() {
172			shortcuts = append(shortcuts, shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "v", Description: "Verbosity", Disabled: inTree})
173		}
174		shortcuts = append(shortcuts,
175			shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "/", Description: "Search", Disabled: inTree},
176			// Beside the search it modifies, and greyed with it: the case is a
177			// property of the `/` filter, and a document has one whether or not a
178			// query is running — so it is offered before one is typed, the way `w`
179			// is offered before there is anything to wrap.
180			shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "s", Description: "Toggle case", Disabled: inTree},
181			// The gutter and the jump belong to the text pane for the same reason as
182			// the wrap: the tree has rows, not lines, and a line number there would
183			// name nothing.
184			shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "n", Description: "Toggle line numbers", Disabled: inTree},
185			shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "g", Description: "Go to line", Disabled: inTree},
186		)
187	
188		shortcuts = append(shortcuts, shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "c", Description: "Toggle coloring"})
189	
190		if _, ok := m.timestamps(); ok {
191			shortcuts = append(shortcuts, shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "t", Description: "Toggle timestamps"})
192		}
193		if m.source != nil {
194			shortcuts = append(shortcuts, shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "ctrl+r", Description: "Reload"})
195		}
196		if _, ok := m.followable(); ok {
197			// The wording says which way the key goes, the way `f` does above.
198			if m.following {
199				shortcuts = append(shortcuts, shortcut.Shortcut{Key: keymap.Fetch, Description: "Stop following"})
200			} else {
201				shortcuts = append(shortcuts, shortcut.Shortcut{Key: keymap.Fetch, Description: "Follow live output"})
202			}
203		}
204		if _, ok := m.pageable(); ok {
205			shortcuts = append(shortcuts, shortcut.Shortcut{Key: keymap.Pager, Description: "Open in system pager"})
206		}
207	
208		return append(shortcuts,
209			shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "esc", Description: "Go back"},
210			shortcut.Shortcut{Key: "?", Description: "Help"},
211		)
212	}

1	// Package keymap declares the application's keyboard vocabulary.
2	//
3	// It does not read any key and does not depend on bubbletea: it is a list of
4	// strings, and its only role is to be the reference the tests check the code
5	// against (keymap_test.go). Without this reference, key consistency is a
6	// convention that nothing verifies — which is exactly the state §3.26 found:
7	// 184 bindings, 16 collisions.
8	//
9	// # Three disjoint namespaces
10	//
11	//   - An UPPERCASE letter is an action, and its meaning is global to the
12	//     application. `D` deletes, in every view, whatever "delete" means
13	//     wherever you are.
14	//   - A lowercase letter is a filter or a display toggle. It changes
15	//     nothing, so its meaning can be local and two views can use the same
16	//     letter without contradicting each other.
17	//   - Everything else (arrows, esc, enter, tab, space, `/`, `.`, `?`, `:`) is
18	//     structural and never changes.
19	//
20	// # Why Shift carries the actions
21	//
22	// This isn't a matter of taste, it's the real budget of a terminal:
23	//
24	//	Ctrl+letter  : only encodes ASCII 0x40-0x5F, and the tty confiscates
25	//	               four of them (ctrl+i = TAB, ctrl+m = Enter, ctrl+j = LF,
26	//	               ctrl+h = Backspace). ctrl+a and ctrl+b are screen's and
27	//	               tmux's prefixes, ctrl+c/ctrl+d are SIGINT and EOF,
28	//	               ctrl+s/ctrl+q are flow control.           → ~14 left
29	//	Alt+key      : Option is not Meta on macOS unless the user enables it;
30	//	               the application receives nothing.                → 0
31	//	Ctrl+Shift   : the control code erases case — ctrl+a and ctrl+shift+a
32	//	               both emit 0x01. Telling them apart requires the Kitty
33	//	               keyboard protocol or modifyOtherKeys, which bubbletea
34	//	               v1.3.10 does not enable (that's WithKeyboardEnhancements()
35	//	               in v2). And even then the emulator claims them first:
36	//	               ctrl+shift+c/v/t/w/n are copy, paste, tab, close, window.
37	//	                                                                  → 0
38	//	Shift+letter : no constraint. Works on every emulator, every platform,
39	//	               through SSH and tmux.                             → 26
40	//
41	// Shift+letter IS a two-key combination: two fingers, no accidental firing.
42	// It carries the vocabulary not by default, but because the two other
43	// families are crippled or unusable.
44	package keymap
45	
46	import (
47		"maps"
48		"sort"
49		"strings"
50	)
51	
52	// The 23 actions. About forty actions used to exist for 26 letters: the
53	// rule only holds after merging synonyms (Kill = stop and kill,
54	// Delete = delete and remove, Terminal = terminal and shell) and because
55	// display toggles are excluded from the count.
56	const (
57		New      = "N" // Create a resource from this context
58		Edit     = "E" // Edit the selected resource
59		Delete   = "D" // Delete the selected resource
60		Rename   = "M" // Rename (mv)
61		Scan     = "S" // Scan the selected target
62		ScanAll  = "A" // Scan everything (modal: "purge the cache first" checkbox)
63		Fetch    = "F" // Catch up with the source: fetch + fast-forward, or follow a stream
64		Clone    = "C" // Enter clone selection
65		Terminal = "T" // Open a terminal or shell
66		IDE      = "O" // Open in the configured IDE
67		Web      = "W" // Open a URL in the browser
68		Logs     = "L" // Open the logs
69		Pager    = "V" // Open in the system pager
70		Kill     = "K" // Stop, kill (modal: Stop / Restart, or SIGKILL)
71		Prune    = "P" // Remove unused resources
72		Browser  = "B" // Open the multi-registry browser
73		Get      = "G" // Pull (get) the image or tag
74		Auth     = "U" // Login / logout of the registry — toggles based on the row's state
75		Exclude  = "X" // Exclude — add to .gitleaksignore
76		Requests = "R" // Open merge requests · PRs
77		Issues   = "I" // Open issues
78		// Copy is `Y` — yank. The letter was free even though a modal uses it
79		// for "Yes": a modal claims every key before the view sees it, so the
80		// two are never reachable at the same time.
81		Copy = "Y" // Copy the selection's path to the clipboard
82	)
83	
84	// CommandMode opens the command line, from anywhere — including from a
85	// focused text field.
86	//
87	// ctrl+p, and not ctrl+: : ":" is 0x3A, outside the 0x40-0x5F range Ctrl
88	// encodes, so "ctrl+:" never reaches the application. The fallback was
89	// alt+:, which has the opposite flaw: on Terminal.app and iTerm2,
90	// Option+Shift+; emits a literal character and the key doesn't arrive
91	// either. ctrl+p is free throughout the application, is not a tty control
92	// character, is not the prefix of any multiplexer, and its meaning is
93	// already learned — command palette.
94	const CommandMode = "ctrl+p"
95	
96	// actions maps each action key to its meaning. This is the table the tests
97	// check the code against; the table in §3.26 is its readable form.
98	var actions = map[string]string{
99		New:      "Create a resource from this context",
100		Edit:     "Edit the selected resource",
101		Delete:   "Delete the selected resource",
102		Rename:   "Rename",
103		Scan:     "Scan the selected target",
104		ScanAll:  "Scan everything",
105		Fetch:    "Catch up with the source",
106		Clone:    "Enter clone selection",
107		Terminal: "Open a terminal or shell",
108		IDE:      "Open in the configured IDE",
109		Web:      "Open a URL in the browser",
110		Logs:     "Open the logs",
111		Pager:    "Open in the system pager",
112		Kill:     "Stop or kill",
113		Prune:    "Remove unused resources",
114		Browser:  "Open the multi-registry browser",
115		Get:      "Pull the image or tag",
116		Auth:     "Log in or out of the registry",
117		Exclude:  "Exclude — add to .gitleaksignore",
118		Requests: "Open merge requests · PRs",
119		Issues:   "Open issues",
120		Copy:     "Copy the selection's path to the clipboard",
121	}
122	
123	// Actions returns a copy of the key → meaning table.
124	func Actions() map[string]string {
125		out := make(map[string]string, len(actions))
126		maps.Copy(out, actions)
127		return out
128	}
129	
130	// IsAction reports whether a key belongs to the action vocabulary.
131	func IsAction(key string) bool {
132		_, ok := actions[key]
133		return ok
134	}
135	
136	// modalKeys are the shortcuts of a confirmation modal.
137	//
138	// This is a fourth namespace, and it is disjoint from the other three by
139	// mode rather than by case: a modal claims every key before the view sees
140	// it (priority 1 in every handleKeyMsg), so `N` cannot mean "create" there
141	// — the view underneath receives nothing. Same argument as for InEditMode.
142	//
143	// They are declared here because the §3.26 survey had not seen them, and
144	// an uppercase letter bound without a declaration is indistinguishable
145	// from drift.
146	var modalKeys = map[string]string{
147		"y": "Yes", "Y": "Yes",
148		"n": "No", "N": "No",
149	}
150	
151	// ModalKeys returns the modal shortcuts.
152	func ModalKeys() map[string]string {
153		out := make(map[string]string, len(modalKeys))
154		maps.Copy(out, modalKeys)
155		return out
156	}
157	
158	// IsModalKey reports whether a key is a modal shortcut.
159	func IsModalKey(key string) bool {
160		_, ok := modalKeys[key]
161		return ok
162	}
163	
164	// free lists the uppercase letters no action occupies. They are declared
165	// rather than left to be inferred: the next addition must know where to
166	// pick from without redoing the survey, and an action that settles
167	// somewhere other than here is a duplicate that goes unnoticed.
168	// H came back here with §3.47: it used to trace the route, and the trace
169	// was removed because it answered for the Docker VM rather than for the
170	// machine (D57). A letter an action has just freed up is re-declared
171	// free, otherwise it stays reserved for a use that no longer exists.
172	var free = []string{"H", "J", "Q", "Z"}
173	
174	// Free returns the still-available uppercase letters, sorted.
175	func Free() []string {
176		out := append([]string(nil), free...)
177		sort.Strings(out)
178		return out
179	}
180	
181	// Surface is a screen, its files, and the lowercase letters it uses.
182	//
183	// Path is what ties a file to its surface, and it is there so the
184	// declaration is checkable: without it, "these letters are local to this
185	// view" is verified by merging every list, and `l` declared for netdiag
186	// would excuse `l` in the registries. Matching is done on the longest
187	// prefix, so netdiag/ports can narrow down netdiag.
188	type Surface struct {
189		Name string
190		Path string
191		Keys []string
192	}
193	
194	// localToggles inventories the lowercase letters used as display or filter
195	// toggles. They change nothing, so their meaning is local and the same
196	// letter can serve twice without contradiction — `l` is the protocol in
197	// netdiag and the LOW severity in security.
198	//
199	// A file that matches no surface is entitled to no lowercase letter at
200	// all: that is the default, and it is what makes the list worth keeping
201	// up to date.
202	var localToggles = []Surface{
203		{"containers", "ui/containers/", []string{"r", "p", "s", "t", "z"}},
204		{"viewer", "ui/viewer/", []string{"f", "c", "w", "v", "t", "n", "g", "s"}},
205		{"netdiag/ports", "ui/netdiag/ports_model.go", []string{"t", "u", "l", "e", "n", "z"}},
206		{"netdiag/checks", "ui/netdiag/", []string{"p"}},
207		{"oci/browser", "ui/oci_resources/browser_", []string{"r"}},
208		{"security/findings", "ui/security/", []string{"c", "h", "m", "l"}},
209	}
210	
211	// LocalToggles returns the declared surfaces.
212	func LocalToggles() []Surface {
213		return append([]Surface(nil), localToggles...)
214	}
215	
216	// SurfaceFor ties a file path to its surface, by longest prefix. The
217	// second return says whether a surface was found.
218	func SurfaceFor(path string) (Surface, bool) {
219		var best Surface
220		found := false
221		for _, s := range localToggles {
222			if !strings.Contains(path, s.Path) {
223				continue
224			}
225			if !found || len(s.Path) > len(best.Path) {
226				best, found = s, true
227			}
228		}

1	package viewer
2	
3	import (
4		"os/exec"
5		"path/filepath"
6		"time"
7	)
8	
9	// Source is where a document came from, and it is carried rather than the bytes
10	// alone.
11	//
12	// The reason is everything the container logs pane could do that a byte slice
13	// cannot: reload, follow, re-fetch with timestamps. Those are properties of the
14	// *origin*, not of the pane — and a file gains from it too, since a document
15	// re-read after an external edit is the same question as a log re-fetched.
16	type Source interface {
17		// Name is what the header shows.
18		Name() string
19		// Kind is what the producer declares. KindAuto lets the name and the
20		// content decide, which is what a file browser passes.
21		Kind() Kind
22		// Load fetches the content. It runs on a Cmd's goroutine, never in Update
23		// (Rule 110).
24		Load() ([]byte, error)
25	}
26	
27	// The three optional capabilities below are probed with a type assertion, the
28	// same way the router probes FooterView and FramelessView.
29	//
30	// Each is a *single* method on purpose. CLAUDE.md's warning about HeaderView is
31	// that a view supplying two of its four methods satisfies none of it and fails
32	// in silence; an interface with one method has no half-satisfied state to fall
33	// into. That is why these are three interfaces and not one with three methods.
34	
35	// Timestamped is a source that can re-fetch with or without timestamps. It
36	// unlocks `t`.
37	type Timestamped interface {
38		Source
39		WithTimestamps(on bool) Source
40	}
41	
42	// Followable is a source worth re-reading on a clock. It unlocks `F`.
43	//
44	// It returns an interval rather than a command, and that is the whole of the
45	// fix. Following used to hand the terminal to `docker logs -f` through
46	// tea.ExecProcess, and there is no way out of that process but ctrl+c — which
47	// the suspended TUI does not intercept, so it killed DevDesk outright and left
48	// the terminal in whatever mode the child had put it in. Keys stopped answering
49	// afterwards. Observed, not theorised.
50	//
51	// A follow is therefore a re-read on a timer, inside the viewport, which is
52	// exactly what the ports tab already does with `ss`. The source names the
53	// cadence because only it knows what a read costs: a `docker logs --tail 500`
54	// is not a file stat.
55	//
56	// The trade is stated rather than discovered: this polls, it does not stream.
57	// A line can wait up to one interval, and a burst longer than the source's tail
58	// is missed between two reads. `V` still hands the whole thing to the pager,
59	// which does stream — and which the user leaves with `q` rather than ctrl+c.
60	type Followable interface {
61		Source
62		FollowInterval() time.Duration
63	}
64	
65	// Pageable is a source that can be handed to the system pager. It unlocks `e`.
66	//
67	// It survives for logs alone, and deliberately: `less` handles a gigabyte and
68	// follows it, which a viewport holding the whole document in memory will never
69	// do. Every other pager path in the application is deleted by this view.
70	type Pageable interface {
71		Source
72		PagerCmd() *exec.Cmd
73	}
74	
75	// FileSource reads a file from disk. It is the workspaces view's source, and
76	// the only one in this package: the others know docker, and this package must
77	// not.
78	type FileSource struct {
79		Path string
80	}
81	
82	// NewFileSource builds a source for a path on disk.
83	func NewFileSource(path string) FileSource {
84		return FileSource{Path: path}
85	}
86	
87	func (s FileSource) Name() string { return filepath.Base(s.Path) }
88	
89	// Kind is KindAuto: a file browser does not know what it is opening, so the
90	// extension and then the content decide.
91	func (s FileSource) Kind() Kind { return KindAuto }
92	
93	func (s FileSource) Load() ([]byte, error) { return ReadFile(s.Path) }
